document.title: Foundations of Public Health Communication
document.summary: This lecture explains how audience analysis, evidence-based message design, and strategic channel selection combine to produce effective public health communication that shapes decisions and changes behaviour at scale.
learningObjectives: Define target audience and explain why segmentation improves message effectiveness
Apply the four message design principles to a real-world health scenario
Select an appropriate communication channel for a given population and context
Recognise common pitfalls such as false certainty and jargon overload

sections.title: Communication basics
sections.sectionSummaryLine: Why message clarity and audience alignment are the starting point for any campaign.

blocks.text: Public health communication translates evidence into messages that people can understand and act on. Its purpose goes beyond transferring information — it supports informed decisions, shapes health behaviour, and builds institutional trust.

blocks.title: Key definition — Target audience
blocks.text: A target audience is the specific group a message is designed to reach and influence. Effective segmentation considers demographics, values, health literacy, and access to information channels.

items: Who needs this information? — identify the segment precisely.
What should they understand or do? — define one clear call to action.
Which channel can reach them effectively? — match the medium to the audience.

blocks.text: The single biggest problem in communication is the illusion that it has taken place.

blocks.title: Core take-aways
items: Clarity and brevity reduce cognitive load for all literacy levels.
Cultural framing determines whether a message feels relevant or alien.
One message cannot serve every segment equally well.

blocks.title: Section recap
points: Target audiences must be defined before content is written.
Three orienting questions anchor every campaign decision.
Transmission is not the same as comprehension.

sections.title: Message design
sections.sectionSummaryLine: The principles that make a public health message stick — and the traps that make it fail.

blocks.text: Effective messages are accurate, focused, actionable, and appropriate for the audience's language and context. Each of those four properties can be tested independently during review.

blocks.caption: Table 1 — Message design principles
rows: Use plain language; avoid jargon and acronyms.
Connect the message to the audience's lived experience.
Generic framing that ignores local context.
End with a concrete, feasible next step.
Vague calls to action ('stay healthy') that cannot be acted on.

blocks.title: Critical pitfall — False certainty
blocks.text: Do not add certainty that is not present in the evidence. Audiences who later discover over-stated claims lose trust in public health institutions — a cost that compounds over time.

items.title: Define the single action
items.text: State, in one sentence, what you want the audience to do or believe after reading.

items.title: Draft at grade-8 reading level
items.text: Use the Flesch–Kincaid tool or equivalent. Aim for sentence lengths below 20 words.

items.title: Test with a representative sample
items.text: Five cognitive interviews with target-audience members reveal 80 % of major comprehension barriers.

items.title: Revise and clear channel-specific constraints
items.text: Adapt character limits, visual hierarchy, and urgency framing to the chosen medium.

rows.label: Opening
rows.left: 'Get vaccinated by Friday to stay protected this winter.'
rows.right: 'Immunisation schedules are recommended for eligible cohorts.'

rows.label: Certainty
rows.left: 'Vaccines reduce hospitalisation risk by about 70 % in clinical trials.'
rows.right: 'Vaccines completely eliminate the risk of serious illness.'

rows.label: Action
rows.left: 'Book your free appointment at the link below.'
rows.right: 'We encourage the public to consider preventive options.'

blocks.title: flesch_kincaid.py — readability screening helper
Practical tip — Plain-language proxy test
blocks.text: Ask a colleague outside public health to read your draft and explain it back to you. If they introduce a different meaning, the message is not yet clear enough.

sections.title: Channel selection
sections.sectionSummaryLine: Matching medium to audience — and why a mismatch can nullify a perfect message.

blocks.text: Channel selection determines whether a message ever reaches its audience. The best-designed message fails if it is delivered through a medium the target group does not use, trust, or have access to.

blocks.title: Equity consideration
blocks.text: Digital channels systematically under-reach elderly, rural, and low-income populations. Always pair a digital campaign with at least one offline channel to avoid widening health information inequities.

items.title: Audience mapping
items.text: Identify segments, their preferred channels, and trusted messengers.

items.title: Channel strategy
items.text: Select primary and secondary channels; negotiate media slots or partnerships.

items.title: Content production
items.text: Adapt the core message to each channel's format, length, and tone requirements.

items.title: Pilot launch
items.text: Release to a small, representative subset and collect rapid feedback.

items.title: Full rollout & monitoring
items.text: Publish across all channels; monitor reach, comprehension, and behaviour proxies weekly.

items: Local radio in the vernacular language

sections.title: Evaluation & iteration
sections.sectionSummaryLine: Measuring what you said versus what your audience heard — and closing the loop.

blocks.text: Evaluation is not a final step — it is embedded throughout the campaign lifecycle. Distinguishing process, outcome, and impact metrics prevents teams from confusing activity with effect.

blocks.title: Three evaluation levels
blocks.text: Process metrics measure whether activities were delivered as planned (e.g. posts published, leaflets distributed). Outcome metrics measure immediate effects (e.g. message recall, attitude change). Impact metrics measure long-term behaviour change (e.g. vaccination uptake rates).

blocks.title: Message reach efficiency
blocks.description: Expresses cost-per-thousand unique exposures (CPM). Lower values indicate more efficient reach. Compare across channels within the same campaign.

items.definition: The number of unique individuals exposed to the message at least once.
The average number of times a reached individual is exposed to the message.
The proportion of exposed individuals who can accurately restate the key message without prompting.
The mental effort required to process and retain a message; excess load impairs comprehension.

blocks.title: Best practice — Feedback loop
blocks.text: Plan your evaluation method before content production starts. Retrofitting evaluation after launch makes it impossible to establish a baseline for comparison.

blocks.title: Section recap
points: Distinguish process, outcome, and impact metrics before the campaign begins.
Reach efficiency (CPM) enables fair channel comparison.
Recall rates are the most direct test of message clarity.

glossary.definition: The degree to which individuals can obtain, process, and understand basic health information and services needed to make appropriate health decisions.
The way information is presented — emphasising gains or losses — to influence how an audience interprets and responds to a health message.
Low- and middle-income country, as classified by World Bank GNI per capita thresholds.
